title: What is the difference between log retention and log compaction?
shortTitle: Log retention versus log compaction in Kafka

s1_definition.profdef: Log retention and log compaction are two different cleanup policies that control how Kafka decides which records in a partition to keep and which to remove. Time-and-size based retention deletes whole log segments once they exceed a configured age or size, regardless of their keys — it keeps a recent window of the full event history. Log compaction instead keeps, for each distinct message key, at least the latest record with that key and removes older records for the same key — it keeps the most recent state per key indefinitely. Retention answers "keep the last N days of events," while compaction answers "keep the latest value for every key."
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India keeps a log of balance updates. With retention, the bank keeps every update slip for the last seven days and then shreds the older slips in batches — you see the recent history but eventually old slips are gone. With compaction, the bank keeps only the most recent balance slip for each account and shreds the older slips for that same account — so for account SAV2001 you always have the latest balance, forever, but not the full history of every change. Retention is a rolling window of events; compaction is a current snapshot per key.
s1_definition.oneliner: Retention deletes old records by age or size; compaction keeps the latest record per key and removes older ones.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Log retention and log compaction are two different cleanup policies that control how Kafka decides which records in a partition to keep and which to remove. Time-and-size based retention deletes whole log segments once they exceed a configured age or size, regardless of their keys — it keeps a recent window of the full event history. Log compaction instead keeps, for each distinct message key, at least the latest record with that key and removes older records for the same key — it keeps the most recent state per key indefinitely. Retention answers "keep the last N days of events," while compaction answers "keep the latest value for every key."

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India keeps a log of balance updates. With retention, the bank keeps every update slip for the last seven days and then shreds the older slips in batches — you see the recent history but eventually old slips are gone. With compaction, the bank keeps only the most recent balance slip for each account and shreds the older slips for that same account — so for account SAV2001 you always have the latest balance, forever, but not the full history of every change. Retention is a rolling window of events; compaction is a current snapshot per key.

**One line to remember:** Retention deletes old records by age or size; compaction keeps the latest record per key and removes older ones.

sections.s2_technical:
Every Kafka topic has a cleanup policy set by `cleanup.policy`, which can be `delete` (retention), `compact` (compaction), or `compact,delete` (both). This choice fundamentally changes what the partition stores over time.

Time-and-size retention is the default and is configured with `retention.ms` (how long to keep records, for example seven days) and `retention.bytes` (maximum partition size). Kafka stores a partition as a series of segment files. When the oldest segment's records exceed the retention time, or the partition exceeds the retention size, Kafka deletes that whole segment. Retention does not look at keys at all; it simply removes old data in bulk. This is ideal for event streams where you want a recent window of the complete history and are happy for old events to age out — transaction event feeds, logs, and metrics typically use retention.

Log compaction is a different model configured with `cleanup.policy=compact`. The log cleaner background thread scans the partition and, for each distinct key, retains the most recent record and removes older records with the same key. The result is that the partition always holds the latest value for every key that has ever been written, so it acts like a durable key-value snapshot. A special case is a record with a key and a null value, called a tombstone, which signals deletion — compaction keeps the tombstone for a configured period so consumers learn the key was removed, then eventually purges it. Compaction is ideal for state topics where you only care about the current value per key: current account balances, latest customer profiles, configuration, and the internal `__consumer_offsets` topic, which is itself compacted.

A key behavioral difference is history versus state. Retention preserves ordering and the full sequence of events within the retained window, so a consumer replaying gets every event that happened recently. Compaction does not preserve every event; it may remove intermediate updates, so a consumer replaying a compacted topic sees only the latest value per key, not the step-by-step history. If you need both — recent full history and an eventual compacted snapshot — you use `compact,delete`, which compacts and also deletes records older than the retention time.

Compaction has operational details worth knowing. There is always a portion at the head of the log, the active segment and recently written records, that has not yet been compacted, so very recent duplicates for a key may still be present until the cleaner runs. The `min.cleanable.dirty.ratio` controls how aggressively the cleaner runs, and `delete.retention.ms` controls how long tombstones survive. Compaction guarantees that a consumer reading the whole topic will eventually see the latest value for each key, which is exactly what you need to rebuild state.

The senior-level nuance is matching the policy to the data's meaning. Event topics — "a transfer happened" — are historical facts, so they use retention with a window sized to your replay and compliance needs. State topics — "the current balance of this account" — are latest-value-per-key, so they use compaction to bound storage while always keeping the current state. A classic pattern is event sourcing plus a compacted state topic: the raw events live in a retention topic for audit and replay, while a derived compacted topic holds the current materialized state for fast lookups. Choosing wrongly is costly — compacting an event topic would silently drop intermediate transactions, and using plain retention for a state topic would eventually delete the only copy of a current balance.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India has two kinds of topics with very different cleanup needs, and the team must apply the right policy to each.

Problem 1 — The transaction event feed records every debit and credit as a historical fact, and the bank needs the last seven days for replay and audit but can let older events age out. This is exactly time-based retention — keep a rolling window of the full event history.

Problem 2 — The account-balance topic should always hold the current balance for each account, bounded in size, without keeping every past balance. This is exactly log compaction — keep only the latest record per account key.

Problem 3 — When an account is closed, downstream consumers must learn the account's balance key is gone. This is exactly a compaction tombstone — a key with a null value that marks deletion.

The mini-project simulates both policies. We build a `Record` domain object with a key and value, a `RetentionLog` that drops records older than a retention window, a `CompactedLog` that keeps only the latest value per key and honors tombstones, and a `CleanupDemo` runner. The demo writes several balance updates and transaction events, then applies retention to the event feed and compaction to the balance topic, logging what survives each policy.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile and run the demo
javac com/bank/cleanup/demo/CleanupDemo.java
java com.bank.cleanup.demo.CleanupDemo

# Event feed: retention 7 days (delete policy)
kafka-configs.sh --alter --entity-type topics --entity-name transactions \
  --add-config cleanup.policy=delete,retention.ms=604800000 --bootstrap-server kafka1:9092
# Balance topic: compaction
kafka-configs.sh --alter --entity-type topics --entity-name account-balances \
  --add-config cleanup.policy=compact --bootstrap-server kafka1:9092
```
sections.s5_journey:
The input is three transaction events on the event feed and five balance records on the balance topic, with a logical current time of 1000 units.

Step 1 — On the event feed, three records are appended: an old DEBIT for SAV2001 at time 990, a recent CREDIT for SAV2001 at 998, and a recent DEBIT for CUR3001 at 999. The retention window is five units, so the cutoff is time 995.

Step 2 — Retention runs on the event feed. The old DEBIT at 990 is before the cutoff of 995, so it is deleted. The two recent records at 998 and 999 are after the cutoff, so they survive. Retention ignored the keys entirely; it only looked at age. The feed now holds the last few events.

Step 3 — On the balance topic, five records are appended: three balances for SAV2001 (1000000, then 950000, then 958000) at increasing times, one balance for CUR3001 (250000), and finally a tombstone for CUR3001 with a null value marking the account closed.

Step 4 — Compaction runs on the balance topic. For key SAV2001 it keeps only the latest record, balance 958000, discarding the two older balances. For key CUR3001 the latest record is the tombstone, so compaction removes the CUR3001 key entirely, signaling the account is deleted.

Step 5 — The logs show the event feed keeping a recent window regardless of key, and the balance topic keeping exactly one latest value per key with the closed account removed by tombstone. This directly contrasts retention, which keeps recent history, with compaction, which keeps the latest state per key.

```
2026-10-24 20:38:00 [INFO] [transactions] RETENTION deleted (too old) SAV2001=DEBIT 50000 @t990
2026-10-24 20:38:00 [INFO] [transactions] after retention keeps: [SAV2001=CREDIT 8000 @t998, CUR3001=DEBIT 1500 @t999]
2026-10-24 20:38:00 [INFO] [account-balances] COMPACTION key CUR3001 deleted via tombstone
2026-10-24 20:38:00 [INFO] [account-balances] after compaction keeps latest-per-key: [SAV2001=balance=958000 @t999]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  EVENT FEED (cleanup.policy=delete)         BALANCE TOPIC (cleanup.policy=compact)
  ──────────────────────────────────        ─────────────────────────────────────

  append (by time):                          append (by key, latest wins):
   SAV2001 DEBIT 50000 @t990 (old)            SAV2001 balance=1000000 @t991
   SAV2001 CREDIT 8000 @t998                  SAV2001 balance=950000  @t994
   CUR3001 DEBIT 1500  @t999                  SAV2001 balance=958000  @t999 ← keep
    │                                          CUR3001 balance=250000  @t995
    ▼ runRetention(now=1000, window=5)         CUR3001 <tombstone>     @t1000 ← delete key
   cutoff = 995                                 │
   drop @t990 (too old)                         ▼ runCompaction()
   keep @t998, @t999                           keep latest per key:
                                                 SAV2001 → balance=958000
  Result: recent WINDOW of events               CUR3001 → removed (tombstone)
  (keys irrelevant)                           Result: current STATE per key
```

```
  ═══ LLD — RetentionLog + CompactedLog ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Strategy: cleanup policy (delete vs compact) per topic       │
  │    WHY: same log, different survival rule                    │
  │ Null Object (Tombstone): null value marks deletion           │

  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: RetentionLog ages out; CompactedLog keeps latest-per-key  │
  │ O: new policy = new log class, callers unchanged             │
  │ L: both are logs with append + cleanup behavior              │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ───────────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌──────────────────────────────┐      ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │         RetentionLog          │      │         CompactedLog          │
  │ - topic, retentionWindow      │      │ - topic                       │
  │ - records: List<Record>       │      │ - records: List<Record>       │
  │ ──────────────────────────────│      │ ──────────────────────────────│
  │ + append(record): void        │      │ + append(record): void        │
  │ + runRetention(now): void     │      │ + runCompaction(): void       │
  │   drop ts < now-window        │      │   keep latest per key;        │
  │   (ignore key)                │      │   tombstone removes key       │
  └──────────────┬────────────────┘      └──────────────┬────────────────┘
                 │ contains                              │ contains
                 ▼                                       ▼
              ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
              │                  Record                       │
              │ - key: String                                 │
              │ - value: String (null => tombstone)           │
              │ - timestamp: long                             │
              │ + isTombstone(): boolean                      │
              └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: a record ────────────────────────────────────

  RETENTION:  [LIVE] → age > window → [DELETED]
  COMPACTION: [LIVE] → newer record same key arrives → [SUPERSEDED/REMOVED]
              [TOMBSTONE] → key removed → tombstone purged after delete.retention.ms

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ─────────────────────────────────

  1. eventFeed.append(x3); eventFeed.runRetention(now=1000)
  2.   → drop @t990 (older than cutoff 995); keep @t998,@t999
  3. balances.append(x5); balances.runCompaction()
  4.   → SAV2001 keep latest balance=958000
  5.   → CUR3001 latest is tombstone → remove key

  Contract for runCompaction():
    Pre:  records have stable keys
    Post: at most one (latest) record per key; tombstoned keys removed
    Guarantee: current value per key is preserved
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Log retention and log compaction are two different cleanup policies in Kafka that decide which records a partition keeps. Time-and-size retention, which is the default, deletes whole log segments once they are older than retention.ms or the partition exceeds retention.bytes, completely ignoring the record keys. It keeps a rolling window of the full event history. Log compaction instead keeps, for each distinct key, at least the most recent record and removes older records with the same key, so the partition becomes a durable latest-value-per-key snapshot.

The fundamental difference is history versus state. Retention preserves the full ordered sequence of events within the retained window, so replaying gives you every recent event. Compaction does not preserve every event; it may drop intermediate updates, so replaying a compacted topic gives you only the current value per key. Compaction also supports tombstones, a record with a key and a null value, which marks that key as deleted so consumers learn the key is gone before the tombstone is eventually purged.

You match the policy to what the data means. Event topics are historical facts — a transfer happened — so they use retention with a window sized for replay and compliance. State topics are current values — this account's balance — so they use compaction to bound storage while always keeping the latest state. Kafka's own consumer-offsets topic is compacted for exactly this reason. You can even combine them with compact,delete to keep recent history and an eventual compacted snapshot.

In my banking platform at National Bank of India, the transaction event feed uses retention of seven days so we have recent full history for audit and replay, while a derived account-balances topic uses compaction so we always have the current balance per account without storing every historical change, and closing an account writes a tombstone so downstream caches drop it. The senior point I stress is that choosing wrongly is dangerous: compacting an event feed would silently drop intermediate transactions, and using plain retention for a balance topic would eventually delete the only copy of a current balance. The classic pattern is event sourcing — raw events in a retention topic plus a compacted state topic for fast current-value lookups.

---

keyPoints: Retention: time-based (7 days default) or size-based
Compaction: keep latest value per key — delete old versions
Compacted topic: acts as a key-value snapshot store
